To answer that, I suppose I'd have to know what it means to be a Democrat.

From the name alone, I'd imagine that above all else they favor democratic solutions to non-democratic solutions - which is to say that they seek to legitimize force to further the desires of the majority - no matter how slim or fictitious the majority is (as in the case of taxes passed during special elections where a majority constitutes over 50% of 5% of the voter turn-out). In that sense, a Democrat couldn't be a Libertarian.

When we take a broader view though, I think that Libertarian is simply on a different axis than the other two. You really do find Democrats that are rather libertarian on a variety of issues - or maybe vote libertarian for non-libertarian reasons.

I don't think we're likely to have 33% of voters register and vote Libertarian overnight (one reason is that based on the people I know, the longer a person is a Libertarian, the less likely they are to care about voting at all). So the advance of the Libertarian movement rests most heavily on the spread of Libertarian sentiments. This has been happening... slowly... for most of my life - sometimes faster than others. I think it's inevitable - especially as technology spreads and enables people to coordinate activities without a strong central authority.

In the mean time, I'll settle for libertarian leaning R's and D's. I think you see Libertarian R's because they need to run on Libertarian principles to win their elections - or it gives them an edge at least. Democrats may not feel the need to do that. Also, Democrats seem to rely heavily on high taxation - it's really hard to be against the initiation of force for social and political goals and be in favor of taxation at all.

Recently in my town we had a 3-way race with a Republican, a Democrat who was the former Libertarian Party chairman for the county, and a Republican who was running as a Libertarian. Next time, I'd like all three to be Libertarians. After that, I'd like all races to be like that.

Of course, many of the races in my area are still uncontested, so there are a lot of opportunities for Libertarians to get elected - especially in smaller political subdivisions where campaigning is cheap and the races are non-partisan so it's harder for slate voters to have an impact.

Welcome, fellow boxing fans from around the world, to our new boxing community here on voat. The sport of boxing received more glorious time in the spotlight these past few months than at any other point in the past 25 years, and many people are discovering the magic of the sweet science for the first time. Voat is a brilliant, uncensored platform for in-depth discussion, whether you are the most hardcore boxing aficionado or the most casual of fans. Ironically, it is combat that brings us together.

To better familiarize myself with y'all, I am from the fine state of Tennessee, and my home state is better known for whiskey and college football than boxing. I was unfortunately left without someone to cheer for in the professional boxing scene, until Deontay Wilder started knocking out literally everyone he fought. Tonight, Wilder faces challenger Eric Molina in Bartow Arena, only 2 and 1/2 hours south of my home. Being the first American heavyweight champion in almost a decade, Wilder fulfills the role of hometown hero in more ways than one, as he may be the only man capable of dethroning Ukranian heavyweight king Wladimir Klitschko. What makes Deontay special? The answer is his enormous, destructive punching power. Wilder is charming and sincere on camera, but his god-level power leaves his opponents flat on the canvas in 97% of his fights.

However, despite taking Bermane Stiverne 12 rounds for the WBC heavyweight world title, Al Haymon has kept Deontay relatively well-protected, and there is a general consensus that Wilder needs to be tested against tough opposition such as Alexander Povetkin and Tyson Fury before he ascends to Klitschko's mantle. No disrespect to Deontay, but Wladimir is one fight shy of matching Joe "The Brown Bomber" Louis' record number of heavyweight title defenses. Deontay "The Bronze Bomber" Wilder still has some developing to do, and this fight is his first title defense. Tonight's fight against Molina fight won't add much value to his resume or his reputation, but the experience gained will bring him one step closer to future megafights. My official prediction is that Wilder scores an early KO of Molina, maybe even in the first round. Deontay deserves to be in with the best; but for now, he is tasked with dismantling the fighter ranked 44th in the divison. I'm pretty confident that is exactly what he will do; dismantle, and destroy.
THEBOXINGSTAR PREVIEW 6/13/2015 - DEONTAY WILDER vs. ERIC MOLINA

Yeah, but I still need to see more. Especially after the third round against Molina. Sure, Wider got the stoppage, but after being rocked like that by a school teacher, I have my doubts of his chances against Klitschko. Maybe he will get there, but I don't think he is at that level yet.

Yeah, I agree. His defense is very limited, almost one-dimensional, and that chin just can't take a hard punch. Klitschko has a weak chin, too, but he learned to adjust his strengths around it. Maybe Wilder will learn to compensate in a similar fashion.
